title: How lonely or influential is the Lone Wolf? An analysis of individual scholars’ solo-authorship dynamics
short_title: How lonely or influential is the Lone Wolf? Solo-authorship dynamics

affiliations.1: Department of Mathematics, Ariel University, Ariel, Israel
affiliations.3: Department of Information Science, Bar Ilan University, Ramat Gan, Israel

abstract: Collaboration has become a defining feature of modern science. Nevertheless, solo-authorship has not disappeared entirely. In this study, we investigate solo-authorship dynamics at the individual scholar level, a perspective often overlooked in favor of publication-level analyses, focusing on the propensity of scholars to solo-publish over their careers and this propensity’s potential relation to their academic influence. Using a dataset of 7238 scholars from Biology, Computer Science, Psychology, and Philosophy, we analyze the temporal solo-authorship patterns through heatmap analysis, time series clustering, and statistical testing. By formally defining and analyzing the notion of the academic “Lone Wolf” - a scholar who persistently solo-publishes at a high rate - we show that a global definition of a Lone Wolf may seem unreasonable. Nevertheless, we identify three characteristic solo-authorship trajectories across the four disciplines that share several commonalities and highly their differences. Our findings do not suggest any significant relation between scholars’ solo- authorship dynamics and their influence metrics.
summary: Most science is now collaborative, but some scholars still publish alone. Using a dataset of 7238 scholars from biology, computer science, psychology and philosophy, we tracked how each scholar's tendency to solo-publish changes over a career and whether it relates to academic influence. A single global definition of an academic 'Lone Wolf' seemed unreasonable, but we found three characteristic solo-authorship trajectories and no significant link with influence metrics.
key_findings: We formally defined the academic 'Lone Wolf', a scholar who persistently solo-publishes at a high rate, and showed a global definition may seem unreasonable.
Three characteristic solo-authorship trajectories appear across the four disciplines, sharing several commonalities alongside their differences.
We found no significant relation between scholars' solo-authorship dynamics and their influence metrics.
